cue: How do you say someone never puts their hand in their pocket?

es.meaning: To be mean with money; to avoid paying whenever possible.
es.example: Nunca invita ni un café: es un agarrado.
es.exampleTranslation: He's never once bought a coffee — he's tight-fisted.
es.regionNote: Widely used; MX also has 'codo' for the same idea, which is arguably the better MX anchor — reviewer to decide.

it.literal: to have the little arm short
it.meaning: To be mean with money; to avoid reaching for one's wallet.
it.example: Non offre mai niente: ha il braccino corto.
it.exampleTranslation: He never gets a round in — his arms don't reach his pockets.

bridge.note: Italian pictures the moment of not paying: the arm is too short to reach the pocket, so the wallet stays where it is. Spanish pictures the hand instead, closed and holding on — agarrado, from agarrar, to grip. One language shortens the reach, the other tightens the grip. Note what Italian does to the arm on the way: braccino, not braccio, a diminutive that makes the meanness small and faintly ridiculous rather than sinister.

interference.es_to_it: There is no Spanish equivalent of the diminutive doing this work — 'braccio corto' without the -ino is understood but loses the mockery, and the fixed form is braccino. Note also that Italian describes the behaviour with avere plus a body part, where Spanish labels the person with a bare adjective.
interference.it_to_es: 'Tener el brazo corto' is not Spanish. The image swaps to the hand, and it names the person rather than the gesture: es un agarrado. Watch the regional layer too — Mexico has 'ser codo', elbow rather than hand, which is not the same body part and is not universal.

review.notes: ES ANCHOR IS THE OPEN QUESTION. I chose 'ser un agarrado' because it is pan-regional and RAE-listed, but MX's 'ser codo' is at least as common there and would give a THREE-WAY body-part contrast — Italian arm, Spanish hand, Mexican elbow — which is a better entry than the one I have drafted. ES REVIEWER, please decide the anchor; if codo wins, this entry should be re-drafted around it and the bridge rewritten. SATURATION: the bank already has 0071 (ser un manirroto / avere le mani bucate) on the OPPOSITE trait, overspending, and it also uses hands. These two are natural opposites and should not be scheduled near each other. IT REVIEWER: confirm the diminutive is obligatory — the whole second half of the bridge rests on braccino rather than braccio being the fixed form.
